title: Graph lattice sums and graph zeta functions for long-range interacting quantum lattice models
abstract: Taming the exponential increase of the Hilbert space dimension with system size in the simulation of gapped quantum lattice models is of the highest relevance for understanding and designing exotic quantum materials, where nonlocal interactions are of particular interest. High-order linked-cluster expansions provide access the solution of the eigenvalue problem for the infinite system, yet rely on the computation of high-dimensional oscillatory lattice sums with a graph structure, only approachable with Monte Carlo methods so far. This work resolves this issue, rendering all required graph lattice sums, referred to as graph zeta functions for kernels involving power-laws, computable. The resulting method reduces the evaluation time for state-of-the art series expansions from tenthousands of core-hours to minutes. After factorizing the lattice sum over blocks, each block is evaluated by the cheapest available strategy depending on its treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$. Basic blocks admit analytic forms in terms of generalized zeta functions. Series-parallel blocks with $\mathrm{tw}\le 2$ can be computed at linear cost in the number of graph nodes and in the size of the momentum grid using a semi-analytical algebra based on Epstein zeta functions and rapidly decaying Fourier series. Finally, for $\mathrm{tw}>2$, the method is combined with tensor-network bucket elimination yielding polynomial scaling of numerical work and memory in momentum grid size with exponents only growing with $\mathrm{tw}$ rather than with the number of vertices. Through use of FFT, the full momentum grid is recovered at the cost of a single momentum evaluation. We provide a detailed analysis of the precision and runtime of our method against analytic and numerical benchmarks. We further reproduce published Monte Carlo data for the transverse-field Ising model on different 1D, 2D, and 3D lattices, obtaining full agreement.
summary: This paper presents a novel, highly efficient computational method for evaluating complex graph lattice sums that arise in the perturbative analysis of quantum lattice models with long-range interactions. By leveraging graph theory and advanced mathematical tools like generalized zeta functions, the authors drastically reduce computation time from infeasible to minutes. This breakthrough allows for precise theoretical study of exotic quantum materials and their spectral properties.
main_problem: The primary challenge is taming the exponential growth of the Hilbert space dimension when simulating gapped quantum lattice models, particularly those featuring long-range (nonlocal) interactions.
main_result: The authors developed a novel method to compute required graph lattice sums, reducing computation time from thousands of core-hours to minutes, and achieving full agreement with Monte Carlo simulations for the transverse-field Ising model.
method: The method involves factorizing high-dimensional lattice sums over graph blocks and evaluating them using specialized techniques based on the block's treewidth, including analytic forms via generalized zeta functions and tensor-network elimination.
model_or_system: The work applies to general long-range interacting quantum lattice models, exemplified by the transverse-field Ising model on various lattices (1D, 2D, 3D). The theory relies on high-order linked-cluster expansions.
key_observables: Low-lying spectrum, dispersion relations $\omega(\mathbf{k}, \lambda)$, and the dependence of these on the perturbation parameter $\lambda$.
important_parameters: The interaction range (power-law decay), the lattice dimension ($d$), and the treewidth ($\mathrm{tw}$) of the underlying graph structure.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that physically relevant correlation functions retain translational invariance, which is crucial for defining the graph zeta functions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the computed dispersion relation $\omega(\mathbf{k}, \lambda)$ for the 3D LRTFIM, showing high-symmetry points and cuts along high-symmetry paths, confirming the method's ability to resolve the full momentum grid.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of lattice sums, develops the mathematical framework using graph zeta functions, details the computational strategy based on treewidth factorization, and validates the method by reproducing Monte Carlo results for various lattice dimensions.
why_interesting: The ability to calculate high-order series expansions for long-range interacting systems with unprecedented speed is a major theoretical breakthrough, providing access to regimes previously limited by computational complexity.

Low-order corpora of the long-range transverse-field Ising model on an arbitrary d-dimensional lattice Λ, obtained via the pCUT method, where all edges e ∈E are associated with an identical kernel Ke ∈ℓ1(Λ). Panel (a) depicts the corpus for the ground state energy density e0(λ) (no terminals) up to expansion order 7 (up to 6d-dimensional lattice sums), including the graphs G and their prefactors ar(G) ∈Q. Figure 2. Relative error of the zeta algebra for a cycle with |V | = 4, 8, 12 nodes, neighboring terminals, and power-law edge kernels Kν with equal exponents ν = d+σ at k = 0, compared with the analytic benchmark value at k = 0. The dashed lines display the value for σmax = 0, where only a truncated Fourier series is used. Panel (a) shows the integer lattice Λ, while (b) displays the results for the trigonal lattice with n = 64 points per dimension, respectively. The dashed line displays the conservatively chosen cutoff value in σ, after which σmax = 0 is applied.

Figure 3. (a) Graph obtained from a single bridge by applying the operation T, consisting of a multiplication followed by a convolution, four times. (b) Maximum relative error of the associated graph zeta function ζG(k) for Λ = Z on the grid k ∈BZ64 for σ = 1/2 (black) and σ = 1 (red). Open points correspond to the zeta algebra with n = 64 while solid points correspond to the finer discretization n = 1024. The reference is the Richardson-extrapolated truncated sum over the box [−L, L] with L = 10 000, 12 000, . . . , 22 000, evaluated using bucket elimination at the 64 momentum points. The error increases only linearly with the number of operations.

Figure 4. Runtime in milliseconds for evaluating graph zeta func- tions ζG on a complete nd momentum grid for n = 64 and σ = 1/2 on a single core Apple M1 Max core. Panel (a) shows the run- time for a cycle with neighboring terminals as a function of the number of nodes |V |, while panel (b) shows the runtime for the graph obtained from repeated applications of T, as a function of the operation count. The black dots show Λ = Z, while the red squares display the results for the trigonal lattice. The runtime increases only linearly, compared to exponential increase for direct summation.

Figure 5. Relative error of the graph zeta function with edge exponent ν = d + σ at k = 0 obtained from the zeta algebra for Λ = Z as a function of the number of discretization points n for (a) the cycle graph with |V | = 8 nodes and (b) the graph obtained by applying T 4 to a bridge. The black dots show σ = 0.5, while the red dots display σ = 1. The function is evaluated at n = ⌊48 · 2j/2⌉ with ⌊·⌉the nearest integer and j = 0, 1, . . . , 12. The dashed lines show a linear fit against the logarithmized data, with resulting fit exponents shown as captions to the triangle. The scaling is in good agreement with the theoretical bound |n|−(d+σ+2) from Remark 6.7.
